latest_nl_proof:
We prove the two assertions in order.

First, consider the weighted grading on S.

If d = 0, then by the convention in the statement we have S = Q. In this case the only nonzero homogeneous piece is degree 0: namely S_0 = Q and S_m = 0 for every m > 0. Hence each S_m is finite-dimensional over Q.

Now assume d >= 1. For a = (a_1, ..., a_d) in Z_{>=0}^d, write x^a := x_1^{a_1} ... x_d^{a_d}. Since deg(x_i) = w_i, the monomial x^a is homogeneous of weighted degree

a_1 w_1 + ... + a_d w_d.

Therefore, for any fixed m >= 0,

S_m = span_Q { x^a : a in Z_{>=0}^d and a_1 w_1 + ... + a_d w_d = m }.

Let

A_m := { a in Z_{>=0}^d : a_1 w_1 + ... + a_d w_d = m }.

We claim that A_m is finite. Indeed, if a belongs to A_m, then for each i we have

0 <= a_i w_i <= m.

Because w_i > 0, this implies

0 <= a_i <= m / w_i,

hence in particular

0 <= a_i <= floor(m / w_i).

So each coordinate a_i has only finitely many possibilities, namely 0, 1, ..., floor(m / w_i). Thus

A_m \subseteq \prod_{i=1}^d {0,1,...,floor(m / w_i)},

and therefore A_m is finite. Consequently S_m is spanned by finitely many monomials.

These monomials are linearly independent over Q (distinct monomials in a polynomial ring are linearly independent), so they form a Q-basis of S_m. Hence

dim_Q S_m = |A_m| < infinity.

This proves the first assertion: for every m >= 0, the homogeneous component S_m is finite-dimensional over Q.

Now let I be a homogeneous ideal of S. Because I is homogeneous, the quotient S/I inherits the grading, and the degree-m component is the image of S_m under the quotient map pi : S -> S/I. More precisely, the restriction

pi|_{S_m} : S_m -> (S/I)_m

is surjective, and its kernel is exactly I \cap S_m. Therefore, by the first isomorphism theorem,

(S/I)_m \cong S_m / (I \cap S_m).

But I \cap S_m is a Q-subspace of the finite-dimensional Q-vector space S_m. A quotient of a finite-dimensional vector space by a subspace is again finite-dimensional. Hence (S/I)_m is finite-dimensional over Q for every m >= 0.

So both claims follow.
role_in_parent: Provides the finite-dimensionality hypothesis needed to apply the Hilbert-series positivity lemma to the graded quotient ring produced by L4.
statement_nl: Let d be a nonnegative integer and let w_1, ..., w_d be positive integers. Give S := Q[x_1, ..., x_d] the grading deg(x_i) = w_i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then for every integer m >= 0 the homogeneous component S_m is finite-dimensional over Q. Consequently, if I is a homogeneous ideal of S, then for every integer m >= 0 the homogeneous component (S/I)_m is finite-dimensional over Q.

domain_restrictions: For each i with 1<=i<=d: w_i ∈ {1,2,3,...} (positive, nonzero weights)
S = Q[x_1,...,x_d] when d>=1; S = Q when d=0 (so there are no variables and only degree 0 exists)
I is assumed homogeneous so that (S/I)_m is well-defined as the mth graded component of a graded quotient
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Given d≥0 and weights w_1,...,w_d>0, define the weighted grading on S by deg(x_i)=w_i (and if d=0 set S:=Q with only degree 0). Then for every m≥0, the homogeneous component S_m is a finite-dimensional Q-vector space. Moreover, for any homogeneous ideal I⊆S and every m≥0, the homogeneous component (S/I)_m is finite-dimensional over Q.
quantifier_order: For all d (nonnegative integer), for all weights w_1,...,w_d (positive integers), for all m (integer, m>=0): ...
For all homogeneous ideals I of S, for all m (integer, m>=0): ...

witness_dependencies: No existential witnesses are introduced; the claim is purely universal: finite-dimensionality holds for each fixed m with the given d and weights.
In the second part, the ideal I is a universally quantified parameter (no witness dependence stated); finite-dimensionality is asserted for each m given that I is homogeneous.
